# Results

Following the previous study showing that axonal activation of p75NTR by proNGF in basal forebrain cholinergic neurons (BFCNs) triggers local protein synthesis, with both APP and tau among the newly synthesized proteins [@dasguptaProNGFElicitsRetrograde2024], this work asks whether proNGF increases tau in BFCNs and what that increase depends on.

To address this I used three culture systems — filter chambers to separate axons from somas for biochemistry, microfluidic chambers for imaging, and whole-cell well plates for validation (see Methods). I looked first at the protein level: whether total tau increases in the soma and axon, at what time point the increase is strongest, whether phospho-tau behaves differently from total tau, and whether the tau increase depends on newly synthesized APP. I then turned to the mRNA level.

## Confirming proNGF Is Active — JNK Activation

To confirm that the proNGF treatment is working, I checked whether it activates the JNK signaling pathway — which also confirms that the proNGF had not been degraded or cleaved during storage. When proNGF binds p75NTR, one of the canonical pathways it activates is the JNK stress-kinase pathway, which drives the retrograde death signal. JNK is active in its phosphorylated form, so if the proNGF is active I would expect to see more phosphorylated JNK after treatment.

Whole cells were cultured for 5 days in well plates and then treated with proNGF. Twenty minutes after treatment — the peak of activation — the cells were lysed and analyzed by Western blot for p-JNK, total JNK, and GAPDH, and the p-JNK / total JNK ratio was used as a readout of how strongly the pathway is switched on (@fig-jnk). Normalizing p-JNK to total JNK controls for how much JNK is present, so the ratio reflects activation and not just how much protein was loaded.

```{r fig-jnk}
#| fig-cap: "**proNGF activates JNK in BFCN cultures.** (Left) Western blot for phosphorylated JNK (p-JNK), total JNK, and GAPDH (loading control) in control and proNGF-treated whole-cell lysates; the p54 and p46 JNK isoforms are marked at 54 and 46 kDa. (Right) p-JNK / total JNK ratio (arbitrary units), higher after proNGF. Both JNK isoforms show a stronger phospho-signal after proNGF."
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "80%"
knitr::include_graphics("WesternBlots/figures/fig_JNK_blot.png")
```

Both JNK isoforms, p54 and p46, showed a stronger phospho-signal in the proNGF lane, and the p-JNK / total JNK ratio was higher after proNGF (@fig-jnk), indicating increased JNK activation. This confirms that the proNGF is active and engaging p75NTR–JNK signaling, so the tau changes I examine next occur in a system where the treatment is genuinely working.

***

## Immunostaining — TrkB and Tau in Control and proNGF Axons

The following section presents immunofluorescence data characterizing the distribution of tau and TrkB in control and proNGF-treated BFCN axons. The goal was to visually assess how proNGF treatment affects tau localization.

BFCNs express all 3 Trk receptors, TrkB among them. TrkB is the high-affinity receptor for BDNF and is a key marker for receptor identity in this system. BFCNs are cholinergic neurons, so ChAT (choline acetyltransferase) is the canonical marker of cholinergic identity, but it did not yield reliable signal; therefore, only TrkB and Tau channels are presented here (see @fig-trkb-tau).

Characterizing tau distribution alongside TrkB allows us to assess whether neurotrophin treatment alters tau localization or abundance in axons.

Looking at the images, you can see the tau signal outlining the axons in the microfluidic chamber, and how proNGF treatment changes the axon morphology. proNGF treatment makes the axons more fragmented and increases the signal of tau "clumps." This is consistent with the known degenerative effects of proNGF on BFCN axons, which may lead to increased tau accumulation as part of the degenerative cascade.

```{r fig-trkb-tau}
#| fig-cap: "**TrkB and Tau immunofluorescence in BFCN axons — control and proNGF.** For each condition: DAPI + TrkB (AF488, green), DAPI + Tau (AF555, red), and the composite. ChAT staining (far-red channel) was attempted but did not produce reliable signal and is not shown."
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "100%"
knitr::include_graphics("figures/precomputed/fig-trkb-tau-v3.png")
```

::: {.content-hidden}

### Tau Distribution in Axons

A key open question is whether proNGF treatment not only changes tau abundance but also alters how tau is distributed within axons — specifically, whether tau appears as discrete clumps or puncta versus a uniform, even distribution along the axon shaft. To begin addressing this visually, cropped regions of the Tau (AF568) channel from the control and proNGF conditions are shown in @fig-tau-distribution. Ideally, this comparison would let us determine whether proNGF treatment shifts tau from a diffuse to a more aggregated pattern, or vice versa, which would have implications for tau's role in proNGF-induced axonal changes.

```{r fig-tau-distribution}
#| fig-cap: "**Tau (AF568) distribution in BFCN axons — cropped regions from the control and proNGF conditions.** Each panel shows the same channel (Tau, red) at higher magnification to allow visual assessment of tau distribution pattern. Clumped versus even distribution of tau signal may reflect changes in tau organization induced by proNGF treatment."
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "100%"
knitr::include_graphics("figures/precomputed/fig-tau-distribution.png")
```

:::

## p75, Tuj1, and Tau Staining 

As a next step, to better characterize the degeneration of the axons across treatments and to be consistent with our lab's previous work I needed to use Tuj1 staining. Tuj1 (β-tubulin III) is a standard marker for neurons and is commonly used to assess axon morphology and degeneration — fragmented or beaded Tuj1 staining is a clear sign that axons are degenerating. Adding Tuj1 would also let me directly compare how tau distributes relative to the axon structure itself, which is important because changes in tau could reflect either a real increase in tau protein or just a change in where it is located along the axon.

In the next 2 experiments I stained for all three antibodies — p75, Tau, and Tuj1 — simultaneously overnight. The result was very weak and patchy signal for Tau channel that is different from the way it looked when used only with TrkB. The problem arises from Tau and Tuj1 primary antibodies competing for binding at the same locations and interfering with each other, which degrades the signal quality.

Looking at the images (@fig-crops-panels), there is a detectable signal from all three antibodies — p75 in green, Tuj1 in red, and Tau in far red — which confirms that the staining protocol is compatible with all three targets however the signals are of low quality. The p75 staining is present but weaker than expected — in BFCNs, p75 should be strongly expressed all along the axon, so ideally the signal should be more continuous and abundant. The Tau signal in the far red channel is also less defined than in earlier experiments, likely, as mentioned, due to allosteric interference between the Tau and Tuj1 primary antibodies.

What we would expect to see with a properly optimized protocol is a clear difference between the control and proNGF conditions: axons treated with proNGF should show signs of degeneration — fragmented or beaded Tuj1 staining, disrupted tau distribution, and potentially increased tau signal consistent with the upregulation seen in the western blots. The control axons should remain intact with smooth, continuous Tuj1 labeling. While the current images hint at some structural differences between the conditions, the signal quality is not sufficient to draw conclusions, and the protocol requires further optimization before these comparisons can be made reliably.

```{r}
#| label: fig-crops-panels
#| fig-cap: "**p75 (green), Tau (far red), and Tuj1 (red) immunofluorescence in BFCN axons — Control vs proNGF.** Each panel: top left Tau (far red, AF633); top right p75 (green, AF488); bottom left Tuj1 (red, AF555); bottom right composite of all channels. All three proteins are detectable, but the Tau signal is weak because the Tau and Tuj1 primary antibodies compete for overlapping epitopes when applied together."
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - "Control"
#|   - "proNGF"
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| out-width: "100%"
knitr::include_graphics("figures/precomputed/fig-ctrl-crops-panel.png")
knitr::include_graphics("figures/precomputed/fig-pronGF-crops-panel.png")
```

## p75, Tau, and Tuj1 — Sequential Protocol

Because the weak Tau signal came from the two primary antibodies competing with each other rather than from a faulty secondary, I moved to a sequential staining protocol. I stained for the primary antibodies of p75 (green, AF488) and Tau (red, AF568) overnight and the Tuj1 (far red) for an hour on the next day before washes and secondaries. The stainings below show clear signal for Tau as well as p75 and Tuj1 in both soma and axons, in the control and proNGF conditions (@fig-if-combined).

![**Sequential staining protocol.** p75 and Tau primaries are applied together overnight; the high-affinity Tuj1 primary is then added the following morning for one hour before washes and secondaries.](figs/TauTuj1SequentialProtocol.png){#fig-sequential-schematic width=80%}

With the sequential protocol we can see that we allow Tau to bind first, and Tuj1 — being very high affinity — is able to bind within an hour afterwards, which allows us to have improved imaging.

```{r fig-if-combined}
#| fig-cap: "**p75, Tau, and Tuj1 immunofluorescence in BFCN axons — sequential protocol.** Control and proNGF axons are shown, each with DAPI + p75 (AF488, green), DAPI + Tau (AF568, red), and DAPI + Tuj1 (far red). Staining was performed using the sequential protocol — p75 and Tau overnight, Tuj1 added the following morning — which rescued the Tau signal lost when all three primaries were applied together."
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "100%"
knitr::include_graphics("figures/precomputed/fig-tuj1-tau-sequential-panel-v2.png")
```

## Confocal Microscopy — Tau Localization Relative to the Nucleus

Given the unexpected observation of substantial tau signal in the soma compartment, I used confocal microscopy to determine whether tau localizes within the nucleus or is restricted to the cytoplasm. BFCNs were immunostained for Tau (red), Tuj1 (green), and counterstained with DAPI to label nuclei (see @fig-confocal-tau).

```{r fig-confocal-tau}
#| fig-cap: "Confocal microscopy of tau localization in BFCNs. Tau (red), Tuj1 (green), and DAPI (blue). Increasing magnification from multiple angles demonstrates that tau immunoreactivity surrounds the nucleus but does not localize within the nuclear compartment."
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "100%"
knitr::include_graphics("figs/Confocal_Images.png")
```

The confocal images at increasing magnification and from multiple angles reveal that tau immunoreactivity is predominantly perinuclear—surrounding the nucleus but not penetrating into the nuclear compartment. This observation suggests that the somatic tau detected by immunofluorescence represents cytoplasmic tau, consistent with tau's role in microtubule stabilization throughout the neuronal cell body.

***

## Time Course of proNGF-Induced Tau Changes

To confirm that axonal proNGF treatment increases tau protein levels and select the best time point for collecting lysates, I treated BFCN axons with proNGF and collected lysates at 30, 45, and 60 minutes. These time points are right before the critical 1–2 hour window during which proNGF induces local axonal protein synthesis, and within which blocking protein synthesis provides protection. After 2 hours blocking protein synthesis no longer protected neurons from proNGF-induced degeneration so the "interesting spike" should have happened before. Western blot results are shown in @fig-sep-combined.

**Conditions:** Ctrl · proNGF 30 min · proNGF 45 min · proNGF 60 min
**Antibodies:** Tau (DyLight 800, 56 kDa) · Actin (DyLight 800, 42 kDa)

```{r fig-sep-combined}
#| fig-cap: "**proNGF time course — Western blot analysis of tau levels in BFCNs.** **(A)** Soma compartment blot: Tau (56 kDa) and Actin (42 kDa), DyLight 800. **(B)** Axon compartment blot: Tau (56 kDa) and Actin (42 kDa), DyLight 800. **(C)** Tau / Actin ratio in soma and axon compartments across treatment conditions. **(D)** Raw band intensities for Tau (top) and Actin (bottom) in soma (left) and axon (right)."
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "100%"
knitr::include_graphics("figures/precomputed/fig-sep-combined.png")
```

**Interpretation:** A progressive increase in tau levels is observed across the proNGF time course, with the most pronounced elevation at the 60-minute time point in both soma and axon compartments. This time-dependent accumulation is consistent with local proNGF-induced protein synthesis occurring within the 1–2 hour window identified by Dasgupta et al. [@dasguptaProNGFElicitsRetrograde2024].

***

## proNGF treatment increases tau levels both in axon and soma compartment  

To test the central claim — that proNGF increases tau — I pooled the control-versus-proNGF comparison across five independent experiments. Total tau was expressed as a fold-change relative to control within each experiment and compartment before pooling; the per-experiment values and the actin/Ponceau normalization details are given in the supplementary material (@tbl-ctrl-pronGF).

Across the five experiments, proNGF significantly increased total tau in the soma, to 1.60-fold of control on average (@fig-ctrl-pronGF; p = 0.027, one-tailed one-sample *t*-test against 1). The axon trended in the same direction, to 1.36-fold, but the increase was more variable and did not reach significance (p = 0.125). The soma is therefore the more reproducible compartment for this effect, while the axon shows a consistent but weaker upward trend.

![**Total tau after proNGF, pooled across five experiments.** Fold-change relative to control (mean ± SEM); each dot is one experiment. Soma (left) and axon (right) were pooled separately. One-tailed one-sample *t*-test against 1: soma p = 0.027 (\*), axon p = 0.125 (ns).](WesternBlots/figures/fig_ctrl_proNGF_n5.png){#fig-ctrl-pronGF width=100%}

***

## Effect of APP Knockdown on proNGF-Induced Tau Increase

Because APP is co-upregulated with tau in the axonal proteome after proNGF, I asked whether knocking down APP affects the proNGF-induced increase in tau. BFCN cultures were pretreated with siRNA against APP (siAPP) before proNGF, and control, proNGF, siAPP, and siAPP + proNGF conditions were compared in both the soma and axon compartments.

To quantify the effect, I pooled three independent experiments and expressed total tau as a fold-change relative to control within each experiment and compartment (@fig-appkd-quant). Because the axonal compartment is actin-poor, I normalized soma tau to actin and axon tau to Ponceau total protein; taking the fold-change within each compartment makes the two normalizations comparable.

![**Total tau across three experiments (n = 3).** Fold-change relative to control (mean ± SEM); each dot is one experiment. Soma tau was normalized to actin, axon tau to Ponceau. One-tailed *t*-tests: \* p < 0.05; ns, not significant.](WesternBlots/figures/fig_siAPP_n3.png){#fig-appkd-quant width=100%}

Axonal treatment with siAPP alone did not cause a significant difference in tau levels from control (p = 0.29), so knocking down APP does not by itself change basal tau. Importantly, proNGF still raised tau when APP was knocked down: siAPP + proNGF was significantly higher than siAPP alone in both the soma (p = 0.037) and the axon (p = 0.012). Consistent with this, siAPP + proNGF was not significantly lower than proNGF alone (p = 0.14). The axon followed the same overall pattern as the soma but was more variable, and the direct control-versus-proNGF comparison in the axon did not reach significance (p = 0.25) although the increasing trend is visible and more experiments are needed to confirm or refute the hypothesis.

Together, these results confirm that proNGF increases tau, and show that this increase persists when APP is knocked down (siAPP + proNGF > siAPP in both compartments). I therefore found no evidence that APP knockdown prevents the proNGF-induced tau increase. This argues against a requirement for APP in the tau response, although a partial contribution cannot be excluded at this sample size. One caveat is that I did not directly confirm the efficiency of the APP knockdown in these experiments (for example, by immunoblotting for APP), so an incomplete knockdown cannot be ruled out as a contributor to the null effect.

A representative blot is shown in @fig-appkd-blot: total tau and Ponceau S (total protein) across the soma and axon compartments. Ponceau S is used as the loading control because axonal actin is unreliable (the same blot probed for actin is shown in the supplementary material, @fig-appkd-actin).

![**Representative APP-knockdown western blot.** Total tau (64 and 56 kDa) and Ponceau S (total protein) across the soma and axon compartments in control, proNGF, siAPP, and siAPP + proNGF conditions.](WesternBlots/figures/fig_2026-07-02_blots_cropped.png){#fig-appkd-blot width=95%}

### Phospho-Tau relative to total tau

I expressed phospho-tau as a fraction of the total tau on the same membrane (pTau / total tau) rather than against a separate loading control such as actin. This asks a sharper question than total tau alone: not whether there is more tau, but whether a larger share of it is phosphorylated. To ask whether proNGF changes this fraction, I computed pTau / total tau for every lane across all the phospho blots I have: February 2026 (two blots — an APP-knockdown blot with soma and axon, and a soma-only follow-up) and the 2026-07-02 blot (soma and axon). Because the blots were probed and scanned separately and sit on arbitrary intensity scales, I expressed each condition as a fold-change relative to that blot's own control, then averaged the fold-changes across experiments, separately for soma and axon (@fig-phospho-quant). Where a proNGF time course was run, the timepoints were averaged into a single proNGF value. One dataset (2026-07-02 soma) had no detectable phospho-tau in its control lane, so its fold-change is undefined and it is left out of the soma average.

![**Phospho-tau summary (pTau / total tau, fold-change vs control) across experiments.** Mean ± SEM of the phosphorylated fraction of tau, pooled across blots and shown separately for soma (n = 2 experiments) and axon (n = 2 experiments); the dashed line marks the control level. Each experiment was normalized to its own control before averaging. The phospho antibody differs between blots (pTau181 for the February blots, AT8/pSer202 for 2026-07-02), so this pools the phosphorylated fraction across phospho-epitopes; the individual datasets are listed in the supplementary material.](WesternBlots/figures/fig_phospho_summary.png){#fig-phospho-quant width=95%}

Averaged this way, proNGF did not change the phosphorylated fraction of tau: pTau / total tau was 1.12 ± 0.23 in the soma and 1.05 ± 0.43 in the axon relative to control — essentially unchanged, with error bars spanning the control level. Knocking down APP (siAPP) slightly lowered the ratio in the soma (0.64 ± 0.03), and siAPP + proNGF sat modestly above control in both compartments (1.26 ± 0.08 soma, 1.32 ± 0.26 axon). None of these shifts is large relative to its scatter, and with only two experiments per compartment they are preliminary. The key point is that the clear total-tau increase with proNGF reported above is not mirrored by a rise in tau phosphorylation (see Discussion).

The phospho and total-tau blots these ratios come from are shown in @fig-feb-phospho-blot (February 2026, soma) and @fig-appkd-phospho (2026-07-02, soma and axon).

![**Phospho-tau blot — February 2026 (soma).** pTau181 (65 and 56 kDa), panTau (56 kDa), and Actin (42 kDa) across control, the proNGF time course (45/60/75 min), siAPP, and siAPP + proNGF.](figures/precomputed/fig-feb2-ptau-totaltau-actin.png){#fig-feb-phospho-blot width=90%}

![**Phospho-tau and total tau — 2026-07-02 (APP-knockdown blot).** p-Tau (pSer202/pThr205; 64 and 56 kDa) above total tau, across the soma and axon compartments in control, proNGF, siAPP, and siAPP + proNGF conditions.](WesternBlots/figures/fig_2026-07-02_phospho_totaltau.png){#fig-appkd-phospho width=95%}

## Effect of proNGF/BDNF Treatment on Tau Levels

Previously in our lab, total protein levels were measured by mass spectrometry in whole-cell lysates. Because this reports the total protein pool, just as Western blotting does, the results below are directly comparable to it.

For tau, the short isoform was detected, and both it and APP changed very little across treatments (@tbl-mapt-total-ms):

| Protein | ProNGF | BDNF | proNGF+BDNF |
|:--|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| Tau | +1.13 (p=0.49) | −1.01 (p=0.95) | +1.09 (p=0.64) |
| App | +1.02 (p=0.74) | −1.01 (p=0.84) | +1.02 (p=0.82) |

: Total-proteome fold change of the short tau isoform and APP by treatment, measured by mass spectrometry in whole-cell lysates (*n* = 3 per condition; fold change relative to control, IPA convention). {#tbl-mapt-total-ms}

These whole-cell numbers differ from the newly synthesized (nascent) proteome measured separately in the soma and axon: there, proNGF raises APP synthesis in both compartments, especially the soma, while tau synthesis moves in opposite directions — up in the axon and down in the soma (@tbl-mapt-nascent):

| Protein | Axon | Soma |
|:--|:--:|:--:|
| Tau | +1.10 (p=0.38) | −1.11 (p=0.56) |
| App | +1.20 (p=0.24) | +1.70 (p=0.50) |

: Nascent (newly synthesized) proteome fold change of the short tau isoform and APP after proNGF, measured by mass spectrometry of puromycin-tagged proteins in separated axon and soma compartments (*n* = 3 per compartment; proNGF relative to control, IPA convention). {#tbl-mapt-nascent}

The axonal treatment with proNGF is very different from whole-cell treatment. Although the total pool of tau and APP moves very little in whole cells, when looking at the compartments separately, APP synthesis is clearly higher after proNGF in both compartments, and the tau signal is increased in the axon while being decreased in the soma. 

To compare the neurotrophins directly, I examined how a 90-minute treatment of the soma with proNGF, BDNF, or their combination affects tau levels in both axons and soma. BFCNs were treated with proNGF, BDNF, or proNGF + BDNF, and tau and actin were quantified in both compartments by Western blot (see @fig-jul25-combined).

**Conditions:** Ctrl · proNGF · BDNF · proNGF + BDNF
**Compartments:** Soma (lanes 1–4) · Axon (lanes 5–8)
**Antibody:** Tau (DyLight 800, 56 kDa) · Actin (DyLight 800, 42 kDa)

```{r fig-jul25-combined}
#| fig-cap: "**Effect of neurotrophin treatment on tau levels in BFCNs.** **(A)** Western blot showing Tau (56 kDa) and Actin (42 kDa) across all conditions and compartments; lanes 1–4 = Soma, lanes 5–8 = Axon. **(B)** Tau / Actin ratio in soma and axon compartments."
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "100%"
knitr::include_graphics("figures/precomputed/fig-jul25-combined.png")
```

This experiment shows that the neurotrophins have an effect similar to the trend seen in the previous proteomics data, which showed that BDNF attenuates the increase in tau. ProNGF-treated neurons show higher tau levels relative to both the BDNF-only and combined proNGF + BDNF conditions, suggesting that proNGF selectively promotes tau accumulation and that BDNF may partially counteract this effect.

***

## ddPCR Quantification of Tau mRNA in Axon and Soma Compartments

### Background and Rationale

The proteomic analysis of the nascent axonal proteome identified two distinct tau isoforms in the soma — 0N3R and 0N4R — while only a single isoform, 0N3R, was detected as newly synthesized in the axon compartment. This suggests that either 0N3R mRNA is preferentially localized to axons, or that 0N3R is selectively translated in the axon even when 0N4R mRNA is also present there. To begin addressing whether this selectivity occurs at the mRNA level, I used ddPCR to quantify total tau mRNA in axon and soma fractions separately, and to ask whether proNGF treatment affects mRNA abundance in each compartment.

### Primer Validation

To confirm that the tau primers amplify reliably from both compartments, I first ran conventional RT-PCR on soma and axon lysates from filter chamber cultures. The primers were designed in the 5' UTR region of the rat *Mapt* transcript, which is shared between the 0N3R and 0N4R isoforms, so this assay detects total tau mRNA rather than either isoform specifically. Both compartments produced a band of the expected size, confirming that the primers work in the filter chamber material and that tau mRNA is present in the axon fraction — consistent with the proteomic evidence that tau is locally synthesized there.

### ddPCR Results

Following primer validation, I ran ddPCR on filter chamber axon and soma lysates from proNGF-treated and control neurons, using beta-actin as a co-loaded reference gene on the same plate. The raw copy number concentrations measured are summarized below:

| Compartment | Condition | Tau (copies/µL) | Actin (copies/µL) |
|-------------|-----------|-----------------|-------------------|
| Soma | Control | 202.70 | 481.51 |
| Soma | proNGF | 308.78 | 1,019.05 |
| Axon | Control | 16.91 | 52.43 |
| Axon | proNGF | 171.43 | 944.33 |

Looking at the raw Tau numbers, there is a clear and large increase in tau mRNA in the axon fraction following proNGF treatment — axon Tau copies go from 16.91 to 171.43, roughly a 10-fold increase. In the soma the increase is more modest, from 202.70 to 308.78, approximately 1.5-fold. This is consistent with the western blot data showing that tau protein increases more prominently in the axon compartment after proNGF treatment.

### Problem: Actin as a Normalization Control

However, when I normalized Tau to actin, a problem emerged: actin itself changed dramatically with treatment. In the axon it went from 52.43 copies/µL in the control to 944.33 in proNGF — an 18-fold difference — and in the soma it roughly doubled. This is far more than expected for a housekeeping gene, and normalizing tau to actin produces a result that contradicts the protein data (tau appearing to go *down* in the proNGF axon). Because of this, the current ddPCR data cannot give a reliable quantitative answer about whether tau mRNA changes after proNGF; the likely reasons and the planned fixes are covered in the Discussion.

### What the Data Does Confirm

Despite the normalization problem, the ddPCR data confirms a few useful things. Tau mRNA is detectable in the axon compartment of filter chamber cultures, which is not trivial given the small volume and low mRNA abundance of the axon fraction. The 5' UTR primers work reliably in this material. And under control conditions the soma has roughly 12 times more tau copies per µL than the axon (202.70 vs 16.91), consistent with the cell body being the primary site of mRNA abundance and the axon holding a smaller, localized pool.
